reports.note: The week the concentration finally broke. SRPT — roughly 30% of the book for three weeks — was called away on the Aug 7 expiry, taking cash from 1.7% to 30.8% and putting every dial back inside its limit for the first time. That is the single most useful thing done all quarter. It does not earn an A: mid-week the reserve sat at 1.7% against a 10% floor, and SPCX was added to below carry while already deep in a loss — averaging down a broken thesis, which is prohibited outright. The week closed clean because an expiry landed, not because the book was run that way. +3.1% on the week.

dials.rule: Top name under the 20% cap · three names above 15%
Back above the 10% floor after the NU assignment · sat at 0.7% mid-week

reports.note: All three dials closed clean. They did not stay clean. The 30.8% reserve taken off the SRPT exit was committed across three sessions into NU, NIQ, XNDU, PLTR, SPCX and BBAI, running cash to 0.7% and gross to 1.09× by midweek. Friday's expiry reversed it: the NU $15 calls were assigned, 300 shares called away at the strike, reserve rebuilt to 16.7%, book back under 1×. Credit where it is due — that exit was pre-arranged by the covered call, the strategy working as designed. But the floor was breached for two days first, and that was a decision, not an accident. +3.2% on the week, the cap held, the sleeve stayed shut.

dials.rule: Top name under the 20% cap once NIQ was called away
Back above the 10% floor on the NIQ assignment · sat at 2.4% into the weekend

reports.note: The NIQ $15 calls assigned overnight — 300 shares called away at the strike, $4,500 back in the account — and all three dials close clean: top name 16.4%, cash 18.8%, gross back to 0.90×. That is the wheel doing exactly what it is built to do, and it is the second week running that an assignment has repaired the reserve. It is also the second week running that the reserve was spent before the assignment arrived: cash ran to 2.4% and gross to 1.14× on Monday and Tuesday, into a new 500-share KEEL position and more PLTR, against money that had not settled. The grade is held down by SERV, where 200 shares were added at 4.87 to 4.90 into a name already 17% underwater. Averaging down a broken thesis is prohibited outright, no dial catches it, and it is the one thing here that was not rescued by an expiry. GRPN's calls were also rolled down from the $40 strike to $23 and $26, capping the recovery on a name 27% below cost. −2.6% on the week.

79 forecast trades across ForecastX and Kalshi — sanctioned for data collection, not scored

reports.note: The cap held and nothing else did. Cash finished the week at $60 — 0.2% of NAV — with stock at 101.5% of net asset value, meaning the book is carrying borrowed money against a 10% floor. Into that, four new names were opened: PR, VSXY, HUN and OLN. Opening positions is a choice; opening four of them on margin with no reserve is the pattern this report card exists to catch. SPCX was also added to below carry for the third time in six weeks — averaging down a broken thesis, prohibited outright, and by now a habit rather than a lapse. The forecast sleeve came back on hard, 79 trades across ForecastX and Kalshi, and is deliberately not scored: it is sanctioned as data collection ahead of building the forecast algorithm. +1.6% on the week, and PLTR at 19.1% is the closest the top name has come to the cap without breaching it.

dials.rule: Inside the 20% cap · SPCX close behind at 17.9%
Third week under the 10% floor · off margin, but stock is 99.8% of NAV
15 forecast trades on ForecastX — sanctioned for data collection, not scored

reports.note: A quiet week that fixed nothing. Not one equity trade was placed in five sessions — no new names, no averaging down, none of last week's escalation repeated, and the book came off margin. That is the improvement, and it is real. What did not change is the reserve: cash closed at $160, 0.6% of NAV, a third consecutive week under the 10% floor, with stock at 99.8% of net asset value. Being fully invested is not the same as being on margin, but it leaves nothing to deploy and nothing to absorb a shock. The quieter problem is the engine. Short calls on BBAI, KEEL, SERV and XNDU all came off at zero in Friday's expiry processing and none were rewritten, so ten of twelve names now sit as uncovered stock. Covered-call premium is the one line in this book with a real edge, and for most of the collateral it is currently switched off. −1.1% on the week; the forecast sleeve ran 15 trades for data and is not scored.

buckets.name: Covered-call premium
buckets.note: The engine. Premium taken on shares already held — managed, rolled, and bought back cheap. This is the line that pays.

buckets.name: Share legs
buckets.note: Where the casualties are. A small number of oversized names, not a failure of selection.

buckets.name: Event contracts
buckets.note: High-volume churn at break-even, negative once costs are counted. Decommissioned — activity mistaken for work.

insights: Loss asymmetry is the leak. The average loser runs 1.7× the average winner, so a 60% hit rate still finishes behind. The targets are being picked correctly; the losses are being let off the leash.
The engine is real: covered-call premium takes 78% of its closes at a 3.8 profit factor across 165 closes. That is the business. Everything else is management around it.

The forecast sleeve is running again, on purpose. It was shut in August after accounting for 90% of all closes and effectively none of the contribution; it reopened on Aug 24 across ForecastX and Kalshi to gather clean data for a systematic strategy in build. Judge it on what it returns once that record exists, not on the churn that came before.

Share legs run a 0.27 profit factor across 34 closes, nearly all of it traceable to two names held past their stops. The per-name cap is scar tissue from this line, and it was breached again this week.

The ledger moves on the back office's schedule, not the market's. NU's August assignment only reached the trade feed a week after the fact, lifting profit factor from 0.88 to 0.91 and the share-leg line from 0.23 to 0.27. NIQ's assignment followed the same path. Expect the forecast sleeve's current run to land in these figures late as well — and do not read any of those revisions as something the market did.

constraints.title: Mandate — what this account may trade
permitted: Selling covered calls against held shares
constraints.note: Interactive Brokers restricts this account to selling covered calls. Cash-secured puts — a core strategy in the principal's personal account and the preferred way to get long a name — are not permitted here, and no position is structured to work around the restriction. A mandate expansion is under review pending a business-plan revision.

p: The book is a concentrated set of retail-momentum securities, twelve names, alongside a forecast-contract sleeve running for data. The week placed no equity trades at all: the book came off margin and gross exposure is back to 1.00×, but cash sits at 0.6% of NAV with stock at 99.8%, so it is fully invested rather than reserved. Short calls came off BBAI, KEEL, SERV and XNDU at the September expiry and were not rewritten, leaving only GRPN and KVYO worked for premium. No name breaches the 20% cap; PLTR leads at 18.1%.

ul: Covered-call premium on liquid small-cap momentum names — the engine, currently written on only two of twelve.
Cash is materiel, not an idle balance — currently spent, though the book is no longer levered.
Outright holds taken selectively, sized small, each carrying a thesis and a stop set before entry.
A forecast-contract sleeve, reopened for data collection ahead of a systematic strategy in build.
Single-name cap of 20% of NAV — held this week, top name PLTR at 18.1%.
Gross exposure 1.00× NAV — off margin, but cash at 0.6% against a 10% floor.
Broker mandate restricts options activity to selling covered calls (see The Desk).
Sizing, reserve, and event exposure inspected every week — findings published whether or not they flatter.

concepts.h: What we hold to be true
ul: Harvest premium. Do not chase direction.
Size is the risk lever. The entry is not.
Define the loss before taking the position.
Most of the tape is noise. Separating it is the work.

p: A handful of durable ideas carry the book: asymmetry — small, defined risk against convex payoff; premium taken from names the crowd overpays to insure; and the discipline to accept that sizing, not selection, is where most books are killed.
Looking like a mad hatter today and being right over the long run is the intended outcome, provided the fundamentals underwrite the view.

The watchlist runs across financials, defense, technology, and petrochemicals. Themes under current interest: artificial intelligence, robotics, satellite communications, credit and insurance, and founder-led firms — with several more held off the page.

discipline.h: The largest position is the trader
p: The principal risk to this book is not the tape — it is the person marking it. Conviction that turns into size. A winner that talks you into a bigger bet. A loser held because selling it makes the loss real. Temperament is the position that has cost the most, and the control framework exists to constrain it rather than to trust it.

ul: Concentration — no more than 20% of NAV in any single name. A hard limit, not a target.
Liquidity — a 10% cash floor at all times. Dry powder is a position, and it is the one that buys the dislocation.
Loss control — stops marked before the order goes in, and honored. No averaging down a broken thesis.
Thesis — every position carries one before it is sized. The typical trade runs entry, target, exit; investments are held outright and not collateralized.

p: Positions are marked daily; the limits are tested every Friday in the after-action. Three dials — concentration, cash floor, event exposure — each passed or breached, and the week is graded on discipline rather than on P&L alone. A green week with a breached limit still grades badly. Breaches are not quietly closed out: cash ran to 0.7% against a 10% floor in the week to Aug 14, and that sits in the permanent record next to the +3.2%.

One oversized position gave back months of grinding. The per-name limit, the cash floor, and the stop discipline are scar tissue — written down so the lesson does not get paid for twice. Limits are set when the book is calm and enforced when it is not. That is the whole reason they are written down at all.

This is a single-manager book. There is no independent risk function here and no second line of defence, and the framework does not pretend otherwise. It compensates the only way it can: the limits are mechanical, the tests are identical every week, and the results are published whether or not they flatter. Self-reporting is worth nothing unless the failures appear too.

Pareidolia is the mind's tendency to see meaningful patterns — faces — in random noise. The idea started as a university capstone and was rebuilt for markets: read the world like an operator, keep the fundamentals in hand, and accept looking like a mad hatter today if the long arc proves the read.
No house view and no consensus to hide behind. We form the read ourselves, size it deliberately, and let a written framework — not the mood of the tape — hold the book.

Pareidolia was built from the ground up, on partner capital and no outside scaffolding. The intent was never to stay small — it is to compound a durable, inspectable process into something far larger, one disciplined decision at a time.
